analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing employees and consumers to give up their day in court before a dispute happens.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred companies from forcing consumers and employees into arbitration, never received a committee vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most people sign away their right to sue without knowing it: when you take a job or open a credit card, fine print often requires that any dispute — over wages, discrimination, fees, or fraud — be settled by a private arbitrator chosen under the company's contract, with no judge, no jury, and usually no class action. This bill would make those pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights cases, and would let a court rather than an arbitrator decide whether an arbitration agreement applies. Companies could still offer arbitration voluntarily after a dispute arises, and union contracts would keep their arbitration systems.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and workers who sign contracts containing forced arbitration clauses — cell phone, bank, credit card, employment, and nursing home agreements. They would keep the right to take claims about wages, discrimination, fraud, and defective products to a judge and jury, including as part of a class action, where settlements tend to be larger and the law develops publicly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and nonunion workers with legal claims

how_it_helps.text: It would make any agreement signed before a dispute arises unenforceable if it forces arbitration of employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights claims, leaving consumers and employees free to go to court, including as part of a class.

It would return to a judge — not a privately paid arbitrator — the decision on whether an arbitration agreement is valid, closing a loophole where arbitrators chosen under company contracts decide the scope of their own power.

The bill's findings state that most consumers and employees have little or no meaningful choice about arbitration clauses buried in form contracts, and often do not know they have given up their right to sue.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that use arbitration clauses would lose a system that lets them resolve disputes privately, cheaply, and largely out of public view, and the arbitration industry would lose that business. Defenders of the current system argue arbitration is faster and cheaper for small claims; the bill's answer was that consent must be voluntary and chosen after a dispute arises.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for consumers and employees with small claims, and the bill would remove that option before a dispute arises even for people who might prefer it.

The bill would sweep broadly — covering not just employment and consumer contracts but antitrust and civil rights claims — a scope broad enough that even sympathetic critics of forced arbitration raised concerns about sweeping in disputes where arbitration works reasonably well.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have restored access to court for the disputes that matter most to ordinary people — wages, discrimination, abusive products — at the cost of making some cases slower and more expensive for consumers and employees to bring, and eliminating a faster, cheaper forum that some people do use and occasionally win in. The strongest objection is that forced arbitration's downside is uneven: many claims are small and might fare better in quick arbitration than in court. Weighed honestly, the bill's aim was widely supported in principle but the binding forced-arbitration industry was powerful enough that the bill never received even a committee vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one hearing, and never received a vote, dying when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Franken introduced the bill on May 7, 2013, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The committee held a hearing on the bill in December 2013, but no markup or vote was ever scheduled.
With no further action by the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015, the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use forced arbitration clauses kept the ability to route consumer, employment, and civil rights claims into private arbitration, and the arbitration industry kept its revenue.

for.name: Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 25 cosponsors.

for.name: 25 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, held one hearing, and never reported it out for a Senate vote.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed limits on forced arbitration in prior Congresses and continued to press against such legislation.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-run Senate committee never scheduled the bill for a vote.

industries.industry: Consumer-facing companies using forced arbitration clauses (banks, credit cards, telecoms, employers, nursing homes, debt collectors)
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to force customer and employee claims into private arbitration and shield them from class actions. This is the industry the bill directly targets.

industries.industry: Private arbitration providers (arbitration firms and arbitrators)
industries.note: A large stream of paid arbitration business from consumer and employment disputes would dry up; their revenue depends on the current system the bill would curtail.

industries.industry: Trial lawyers and consumer-rights law firms
industries.note: Restoring court access and class actions would expand the pool of cases consumer and civil-rights attorneys can bring. Note that contingent-fee litigation can be costly and slow, which is the trade-off supporters accepted.
